_doc: Small talk. 'ask' lines are what YOU say ({first} = them, {addr} = how you address them); 'reply' lines are theirs ({first} = you, {addr} = how they address you). Weather words: fair cloudy rain snow fog wind cold hot. Tags set by the topic: stage_none/ploughed/sown/growing/ripe/stubble, year_lean/fair/plenty; fam_both/kids/spouse/alone/young/orphan/lost/expecting; lord_self/loved/liked/fair/resented/hated/cruel/generous/away; self_priest priest_liked priest_disliked priest_fair no_priest devout; ambition_<id>.

ask.t: Fine weather we've had, {addr}.
A pleasant {part}, isn't it?
Not a cloud worth the name. We'll not complain.
Looks like rain, doesn't it?
Grey as a goose, today.
Wet again. The fields will drink well.
Dreadful, this rain. Is it ever going to stop?
We'll be wading to church at this rate.
Cold enough to freeze a man's breath, eh?
Snow! The children will be pleased, at least.
Keep your hands in your sleeves, {addr}, it's bitter.
Hot work in this sun.
Not a breath of air. I could melt.
This wind will have the thatch off the roof.
Windy enough to lift a cow, today.
Can't see my hand before my face in this fog.
A thick fog this {part}. Mind the ditches.

ask: How do you find the weather, {addr}?
A {weather} sort of day, is it not?
What do you make of the weather?

reply.t: Aye, fair enough. A day to get things done in.
The Lord has been kind this week. I'll not argue with it.
The sun on the back is a great cure for a poor mood.
Good drying weather, if you've washing or hay to bring in.
It'll rain by evening, mark me. My knees never lie.
Grey, aye. But grey's better than the wet.
It'll hold or it won't. We make do either way.
Wet, aye, and my boots with it. But the crops want it.
Another day of it and the lane will be a river.
Good for the meadows. Poor for my back and my patience.
The thatch has leaked at the north end since Michaelmas. Don't ask.
My lord's roof, I'm told, leaks nearly as well as mine.
Bitter. The hearth's not been idle these three days.
Aye, bitter. The old folk will feel it worst. Look in on them, if you can.
Snow's fine to look at. It's the lambing I'm thinking of.
A white world, as you say. The children have been out since dawn.
Hot, aye. I've been sweating like a pig all {part}.
Water and shade, that's the cure. Come by the well.
A parching sort of day. God send a shower before the crop suffers.
It's blown the washing halfway to the next parish, and the hens with it.
A wind like that carries sickness and rumour both, they say.
I'd not put out to sea in it, nor up a ladder either.
Fog, and my eyes not what they were. I bumped a cow this morning.
It'll burn off by noon. Fog never stays to hear complaints.
Folk say wolves walk in fog. I keep to the road.
The weather? One does not choose it, {addr}. One endures it.
Weather is the lord of all of us. Even the king.
Spring weather. Never settled, never kind.
Summer, and still I'm not warm. Strange, that.
The harvest weather is all that matters now. God send it dry.
Winter's hard. We'll see who has wood enough by spring.

reply: Weather's weather, {addr}. We take it as it comes.
There's always something in the sky to complain of.

ask: How goes the harvest, {addr}?
Will the {crop} be good this year?
How are the fields doing, would you say?
Is it a good year for the {crop}, do you think?

ask.t: The strips look well, from the road.
Tell me, how do the crops fare this {season}?
Will we eat well this winter?

reply.t: The ground's ready, and the plough waits on the weather. Not long now.
We've the {crop} sown. Now it's God's work, not ours.
Sown and sprouting. The first green is the best sight in the year.
The {crop} is coming on nicely. A few more sunny weeks.
Growing well, aye, if the birds and the wet leave any of it.
Weeding, weeding, and more weeding. The corn grows well, so do the thistles.
Ripe! We start reaping any day. Every hand will be needed.
The {crop}'s standing golden. If you've a sickle, there's work and a meal in it.
The barns will be fuller than they were, if God holds the storms off.
Stubble now, and the gleaners at it. The year's turning.
Harvest's in, thanks be. Now the dues come due, of course.
The strips lie bare. Plough time soon, if the ground thaws.
A lean year, God help us. Bread is thin and there'll be thinner days.
The harvest was poor. I've cut the household's portions already.
We've had worse years than this, but not many. Pray for the next.
A fat year! Every barn is full and the children are rosy.
Good harvest, the best in memory. I could eat a pie a day.
Fair enough. We'll not starve, and that's all I ask.
Middling, as always. Nobody dances, nobody weeps.
Corn's grown in the country, {addr}. In town we buy it, and mind the price.
I see the harvest in the price of bread, {addr}. Nowhere else.
My steward tells me the tithe barn is well filled. That's enough for me.
The Lord gives and the Lord takes away. We give thanks for what He gives.

ask: What's the price of grain these days?
Is everything dear nowadays, or is it me?
How do the prices stand at market, would you say?
Tell me, are things dear or cheap just now?

dear.t: {Good} is dear, {addr} — dearer than I've ever paid. Folk are grumbling.
Dear as gold, the {good}. You'll have to watch your purse.
Ask me about {good} and I'll weep. The price climbs every week.
The market is stripped of {good}, and what's left costs a fortune.

cheap.t: {Good} is cheap just now. Buy while it lasts, {addr}.
A rare bargain in {good} this week; the sellers can't give it away.
The price of {good} has fallen so low the growers are cursing. Good for us, though.
Plenty of {good} about, and prices to match. Make hay while it lasts.

steady.t: Much as ever. {Good} is neither here nor there.
Steady, steady. No one's rich and no one's ruined.
The market's quiet. {Good} holds its price.
Nothing to remark. A penny buys what a penny bought.

lean.t: Everything's dear after the thin harvest, {addr}. Bread most of all.
Lean year, lean purses. The sellers know it and they charge for it.
Prices climb and wages don't. That's all the news there is.
A loaf costs what a shirt used to. God send us a better year.

plenty.t: Plenty about, and cheap with it. A fat year makes everyone kind.
Grain's cheap, ale's cheaper. I'm not complaining.
Prices are low and spirits high. Long may it last.
Never has a penny stretched so far.

ordinary.t: About what you'd expect. A penny buys two chickens, if you haggle.
The usual. Ale's a penny and a half the gallon, if it's good ale.
Fair, fair. A labourer earns his keep and a little over.
No one complains aloud, so I'd say prices are fair enough.
A linen shirt is twelve pence, as always, if you don't mind rough weave.

ask: How is your family keeping?
And your people at home — well, I hope?
Tell me of your family.
Is all well at home, {addr}?

ask.t: How's the family, {first}? I think of them.

reply.t: My {spouseword} {spouse} keeps well, God be thanked, and our {nkids} {kidword} — {kids} — {theyword} growing like weeds.
Well, thank you. {Spouse} works too hard and {kids} eat too much; so all is as it should be.
A full house: {spouse}, and {kids}. Noisy, but I'd not swap it.
We've had our trials, but {spouse} and I and the little ones are well.
It's only me and the little ones now — {kids}. We manage, one day at a time.
I raise {kids} alone. It's hard, but they're my reason for rising.
Just the two of us, {spouse} and I. No children yet, though we pray.
{Spouse} is well. No little ones yet; it's God's gift, and God knows when.
Alone, as you see. There's no one close left to speak of.
I've no one now. I'm used to it, mostly.
Family? I keep to myself. It's simpler.
My parents, {parents}, are well enough. I do as I'm bid and try not to break anything.
Mother says I'm to say "well, thank you" and nothing more.
I've no parents now. I live where I'm taken in.
We lost one in the cradle. A thing one carries all one's days.
A child of ours is in God's keeping now. We speak of him little.
And there's another on the way, by the grace of God.
I'm with child again; the midwife says before the season turns.
You see us every day, {first}: {spouse} frets, {kids} squabble, and the roof still leaks.
The same as ever, {first}. You live here, you know how it is.
Just you and me now, {first}, and we manage.
Your father frets and your mother nags; and between them they keep us fed.
We do as we always have, {addr}. You've no need to ask; you see it with your own eyes.
Same as you know, {first}. Mother frets, Father grumbles, we eat.
Our own kin are well enough, {first}. Have you had word of the cousins?
As you see, {first}. Our house is as we left it this morning.
You ask me that, {first}? You live here too.

ask: What manner of man is {lord}?
What do folk think of {lord}?
How do you find the lord of this place?
Is {lord} a fair master?

ask.t: Is it true what they say of {lord}?

reply.t: Me? I try to rule justly, as God and the king allow. Folk will tell you what they think.
You ask that to my face, {addr}? Bold. I hope you hear what you wish from others.
A good master, God keep him. We've known worse, and so have the next parishes.
He remembers who he's lord over. That's rarer than you'd think.
Fair enough. He asks his dues, but he keeps his word. I've no complaint.
He's not a bad lord. I've seen worse and I've seen none better.
A lord's a lord, {addr}. He does his work and I do mine, and we mostly keep apart.
He keeps the peace and takes the rents. What more should a lord do?
He takes more than his due and gives less than his share. I'll say no more.
Careful whom you speak of so, {addr}. But since you ask: he is no friend to us.
A hard man. I'd sooner not be overheard.
May he rot, and the rents with him. There, I said it.
I pray for him daily. That God may soften his heart, or take him.
I won't answer that. You know what he is.
Hard, but just, they say. He's had a man whipped for less than a theft.
Open-handed, I'll give him that. The poor eat at his gate at Christmas.
He's seldom here, to be honest. His steward minds us, and not as well.
Our lord is a great man, and great men don't ask the likes of me my opinion.

ask.t: How goes it with the parish and the Church?
Do you attend Mass faithfully, {addr}?
What say you of {priest}?
Is the church well kept, in your view?
The Church is a great comfort, I find.
How goes the parish, Father?
You must have your hands full with the flock, Father.
What would you have me do for the Church, {addr}?

reply.t: My duties are many and my flock is willing, God be thanked. Come to Mass, {first}; it will do you good.
The Church is all I have and all I need. Do you pray, {first}?
A good man, {priest}. Reads the Mass clean and doesn't water the wine.
{Priest} has buried my kin and wed my children. I owe him much.
I attend. The sermons are long and the bench is hard, but God is God.
{Priest} does what he must. I do what I must. We rarely trouble each other.
I attend for the sake of appearances. The priest has a sharp eye for who comes and who doesn't.
A greedy man, the tithe-collector. The tenth of everything, and a sermon on top.
We've no priest of our own just now, and God is poorer for it. We make do with prayer at home.
I'm at Mass every holy day without fail, {addr}. A soul needs it.
A sinner prays hardest. I've plenty to pray for.
I've my own prayers and my own pace, {first}. The Church has enough to say without me.
The Church feeds the poor and buries the dead. That's reason enough to keep faith.
Souls are the Church's business. Land is mine. We rarely quarrel.

ask: How goes the work, {addr}?
What does a {ltrade} do all day?
Tell me about your work.
Is the work hard?

ask.t: What are you busy with these days?

reply.t: Hard, but honest. The soil gives back what you give it, and a little more if God is willing.
Plough, sow, weed, reap, thresh — and again. It never ends, and I wouldn't have it otherwise.
Three days a week on the lord's land, and the other three on mine. A man's own strip is sweeter.
Week-work and boon-work, and then our own fields after dark. We sleep when we can.
Cottar's work: a little of this, a little of that, wherever a hand is wanted.
The sheep don't mind the weather, but I do. Still, lambs in spring make up for a deal.
I know every ewe by her face. They don't know me, the ungrateful things.
Iron and fire. Hot work, but there's never a day without something to mend.
A good blade takes a week; a good plough-share takes an afternoon. The plough-share pays better.
Wood doesn't lie, {addr}. A joint is true or it isn't.
Grain in, flour out, and the lord's cut off the top. It's a living.
Folk say millers have a golden thumb. They never say who put the gold there.
Bread at dawn, whatever the weather. I've not slept past four in twenty years.
Thread by thread, {addr}. A good cloth takes patience and sharp eyes.
The trade's all weights and bargains. I've a pound of sense for every ounce of luck.
Brewing: boil, ferment, sell, pray the ale doesn't turn. An alewife's life, in short.
The day is long and the pay is small, but a man at arms eats regular.
Drill, guard, drill, guard. The war, when it comes, will be a relief.
Keeping a household running is work enough for ten. I've not been idle since Easter.
I serve at table, carry water and mind my tongue. It's honest work.
A little Latin, a little reading, a great deal of waiting for people to confess. It suits me.
Herbs and patience, mostly. And the occasional prayer.
Estates run themselves, they say. Whoever says it has never had one.
I help about the house and run errands. Father says it builds character.
Mother says I'm not to be idle. So I fetch and carry.
Work's work. It fills the day, doesn't it?
Can't complain. Well, I can, but it changes nothing.

ask: What do you hope for, {first}?
If you could have one wish, what would it be?
What do you want most out of life?
Do you ever dream of something more?

reply.t: A quiet life and a full table, {addr}. I've no great ambition beyond that.
I want nothing, truly. That is a rare luck, I know.
To be left in peace with a roof, a hearth and good company. That's all.
To rise a little in the world, {first}. Not to be a lord — only not to be walked on.
Every year I save a little, and every year I think: next year, a step higher.
A better station, for my children if not for me.
Land of my own. A few strips that no lord can take back. That's my dream.
To hold a plot free and clear. I'd sleep better, I know it.
A good marriage, with a family that thinks well of us. It's no sin to want that.
To marry well and make my people proud. Is that so strange?
A workshop of my own, with my name over the door. I think of it every day.
To be master. To have apprentices who curse me as I cursed mine.
To be reeve one day. It's a thankless task, but someone must keep the village honest.
The reeve's staff. I know what I'd do with it, too.
A little coin put by, {addr}. Enough that a bad harvest doesn't mean ruin.
Riches. Not for their own sake. For the doors they open.
To be, when my day comes, a soul the Church would call good. That's the real wealth.
A life without a stain on it, if God allows. I fail often, but I try.
A name men remember when I'm dust. A deed, a song, a tale for the fire.
To do something worth telling. Anything.
To leave. This place has given me all it will. I dream of roads.
Anywhere but here. Don't tell the reeve I said so.
A wrong put right. That's all. I'll not say more.

reply: I think of many things. None I'd say aloud.
That is a question for a priest, {addr}, not a neighbour.

reply.t: What more is there? Bread, a fire, a bed. The rest is vanity.
I've seen what wanting more does to people. I'll take what I have.
A good harvest and no quarrels with the neighbours. That's the sum of it.
Hope? I hope tomorrow is like today, {first}. That's rare enough.
One day my children will not bow to anyone but God. I work towards that.
There's a ladder, {first}, and I mean to climb a rung or two before I'm done.
I watch the steward and the bailiff and think: why not me?
To be somebody. Not rich; somebody.
Strips of my own, ploughed with my own oxen. I dream of the smell of that soil.
If I could buy out my dues and hold my plot freely, I'd die content.
Land is the only thing that lasts. I want some.
A croft, a strip or two, a cow. A man or woman could ask for less, but not much.
A good match, with a family that will take my children kindly.
I'd like to be settled, {first}, and well. A name worth marrying into.
My mother says marriage is a trade like any other; I mean to drive a good bargain.
To marry for love, if I can; for sense, if I must.
Master of the guild. A shop, a sign, apprentices of my own. Seven years' work towards it.
I'm saving for my masterpiece, {first}. When it's done they'll call me master.
A craftsman who answers to no one's bench but his own. That's the goal.
I've the hands. I need the capital and the patience.
To speak for the village at the manor court, and be believed. That's all I want.
Reeve is the best a villager can be: the lord's ear and the neighbours' trust.
They'll pick me one day, if I keep my nose clean and my tongue civil.
I've watched the reeve cheat and the reeve be honest. I'd be the honest one.
Enough that a poor harvest doesn't mean a pawned plough.
Coin, {first}. Coin is the only honest friend in this world.
A chest with a lock and something in it. Is that so much?
Money opens doors. I've stood outside too many.
To make a good end, shriven and at peace, with the bell tolling for me.
I'd go on pilgrimage, if I could. Walsingham, Compostela, anywhere.
My soul is the only thing I'll take with me. I try to keep it clean.
To give half my goods to the Church before I die, God willing.
A deed they'd sing about at Christmas. I'd settle for a verse.
I want to be remembered, {first}. Is that so vain?
Anything but the plough and the grave. A battle, a tournament, a name.
I'd like to be the one folk tell stories about.
I look at the road and I think: it goes somewhere.
If I had a horse and a purse, I'd be gone before the cock crowed.
This place suffocates me. I'd leave tonight if I could.
A town, a city, a ship. Anywhere nobody knows my father.
There's a wrong I'll see righted before I die. I'll say no more.
Some debts are paid in blood, {first}, and some in patience. I'm patient.
Hope? That's a big word for a small person.
I hope the rain holds off and the roof holds up.
Ask me when I know you better, {first}.
You're the first to ask in a long while. Thank you.
